red.focus: Reading ancient responsibility without inventing modern negligence
red.summary: Hammurabi's builders and traders were assigned consequences under particular judgments. Learn to separate the text's conditional rule from modern ideas of fault and equal treatment.
checklist: I can identify the facts triggering an ancient responsibility rule
I can distinguish a fixed historical consequence from a modern damages test
I can recognize social status in ancient liability judgments

sections.title: A House Falls
sections.body_md: A provision of Hammurabi's collection concerns a builder whose poorly secured house collapses and kills its owner. The rule records a severe consequence, linking specified construction conduct with a specified result. The first task is to read its conditions accurately: who built, what failed and what harm followed. This is evidence of an ancient assignment of legal responsibility, not proof that Babylonian judges applied the modern negligence elements of duty, breach, causation and foreseeability in every construction case.

This is evidence of an ancient assignment of legal responsibility, not proof that Babylonian judges applied the modern negligence elements of duty, breach, causation and foreseeability in every construction case.

sections.title: If and Then
sections.body_md: The Louvre notes that Hammurabi's judgments commonly use conditional language: if a situation occurs, then a response follows. This form can look like a modern statute, but its institutional context and purpose differ. The text may specify liability where harm occurs to particular persons or property. Its conditions must be read together. A responsible historian refuses to isolate the sentence's punishment while ignoring which status categories the provision recognizes and which facts the ruler chose to emphasize.

sections.title: The Human Consequence
sections.body_md: A builder's work protects a person's home and life. That human stake helps explain why legal orders have long grappled with responsibility for dangerous construction. Yet compassion cannot settle the historical rule or excuse an unjust punishment. Compare the need to protect occupants with the harshness and hierarchy of recorded consequences. The beginner learns two disciplines: identify the legal trigger precisely, and evaluate the fairness of the response without pretending that the ancient text already contains modern standards.

yellow.focus: Roman Aquilian liability and the role of fault
yellow.summary: Study the Lex Aquilia as a concrete source of Roman wrongful-damage liability. Learn how jurists extended its initially narrower categories through interpretation and procedural remedies.
checklist: I can identify wrongful damage under the Lex Aquilia
I can distinguish property damage from broader modern personal injury law
I can explain why juristic interpretation altered practical coverage

sections.title: The Lex Aquilia's Starting Point
sections.body_md: The Lex Aquilia, probably enacted around the third century BCE, addressed certain wrongful damage to another's property. Its well-known first chapter covered the wrongful killing of another's slave or specified livestock; another chapter dealt with other damage to property. The historical categories reflect a world in which enslaved humans were treated as property by law. That fact is indispensable and morally troubling. The provision's scope was not a general modern tort law embracing every person and injury.

The provision's scope was not a general modern tort law embracing every person and injury.

sections.title: Wrongfulness and Fault
sections.body_md: Roman jurists developed the idea of damnum iniuria datum, wrongful damage, and analyzed when conduct should be attributed to a defendant. Their discussions of culpa, fault, helped shape later private-law thought. But translations of iniuria and culpa cannot be treated as timeless equivalents of today's negligence vocabulary. A historian must identify the relevant passage, its era and the legal action. The same word can carry meanings shaped by procedural history and the interests the institution actually protected.

A historian must identify the relevant passage, its era and the legal action. The same word can carry meanings shaped by procedural history and the interests the institution actually protected.

sections.title: Extending an Old Rule
sections.body_md: Jurists and praetors explored remedies for indirect damage and cases outside the statute's original wording. Actions such as an actio utilis or actio in factum could widen practical protection, though their grounds varied. That is a lesson about doctrinal change through interpretation: a legal system can adapt a written rule without rewriting the original text. Whether the expansion was justified depends on how the court reasoned from recognized authority, facts and the legal problem presented.

orange.focus: The modern duty of care emerges from common-law cases
orange.summary: Examine how case-by-case common-law reasoning came to recognize duties toward people outside a direct contract. Study Donoghue v Stevenson as a major illustration without treating its reasoning as universal world law.
checklist: I can state the legal problem in Donoghue v Stevenson
I can distinguish a negligence duty from a contractual duty
I can explain historical growth through precedent

sections.title: A Bottle and an Unseen Risk
sections.body_md: In Donoghue v Stevenson, decided by the UK House of Lords in 1932, the claimant alleged illness after drinking ginger beer from a bottle containing a decomposed snail. She had not purchased the drink herself. The dispute raised whether the manufacturer could owe her a duty of care without a contract between them. A legal-history student must distinguish the alleged facts, the legal principle under consideration and the actual procedural disposition. The decision was significant for duty reasoning, not a final factual trial finding that every allegation was proven.
sections.audio_script: In Donoghue v Stevenson, decided by the UK House of Lords in 1932, the claimant alleged illness after drinking ginger beer from a bottle containing a decomposed snail. She had not purchased the drink herself. The dispute raised whether the manufacturer could owe her a duty of care without a contract between them. A legal-history student must distinguish the alleged facts, the legal principle under consideration and the actual procedural disposition. The decision was significant for duty reasoning, not a final factual trial finding that every allegation was proven.

sections.title: The Neighbor Principle
sections.body_md: Lord Atkin explained a broad principle concerning reasonable care toward people closely and directly affected by one's acts, subject to legal limits. This reasoning helped develop modern negligence. It should not be summarized as a rule that everyone owes everyone compensation for any foreseeable harm. Courts later refined duty principles and placed additional limits on liability. The historical point is a movement toward recognizing responsibilities to people outside contractual relationships, while preserving the distinct legal questions of breach, causation and actionable damage.

sections.title: A Doctrine Has a History
sections.body_md: Donoghue did not erase Roman law, contractual remedies or statutory duties. It sits within a developing common-law tradition and has influenced many jurisdictions differently. When studying later decisions, ask which aspect of its reasoning is binding, how courts distinguished it and which policy concerns altered its reach. A single landmark can change the vocabulary of law without becoming an all-purpose legal test. A lawyer must cite the current governing law, not merely the case's fame.

black.focus: Liability systems and the politics of industrial risk
black.summary: Compare fault liability with statutory and enterprise-based responses to mass production. Evaluate when a rule that looks neutral fails people least able to investigate or insure against industrial harm.
checklist: I can differentiate fault and risk allocation theories historically
I can explain how evidence barriers shaped industrial reform
I can critique liability proposals without conflating policy and existing law

sections.title: Industry Exposes the Limits of Fault
sections.body_md: Factories and mass markets produce injuries involving complex systems, poorly documented decisions and defendants who control much of the relevant evidence. Fault-based litigation can sometimes deter negligence, yet proving an individual employee's breach may be impossible even when an enterprise creates substantial risk. Legislatures in different jurisdictions responded through workers' compensation, product regulation and other mechanisms. The historical lesson is not that strict liability replaced negligence everywhere. It is that industrial organization changed both the pattern of harm and the practicality of proof.

The historical lesson is not that strict liability replaced negligence everywhere. It is that industrial organization changed both the pattern of harm and the practicality of proof.

sections.title: Risk Allocation Has a Price
sections.body_md: An enterprise-liability approach may place predictable accident costs on businesses that benefit from an activity and can insure or improve safety. But a poorly designed rule may overdeterr beneficial work, shift excessive costs to consumers or impose liability unrelated to meaningful control. A doctoral historian compares institutional capacity, evidence costs and the distribution of losses. It is essential to separate a case's present doctrinal elements from the reasons reformers give for changing those elements. Moral urgency does not authorize a court to invent statutory liability.

sections.title: The Best Rule Protects People
sections.body_md: Imagine workers injured by a machine when no single supervisor can be shown to have acted carelessly. A comprehensive answer examines workplace regulation, insurance, possible civil remedies and the actual claims available in that legal system. It also asks who could prevent future harm and who bears the cost of delay. The goal is not maximum punishment. It is a rule that promotes safety, offers fair redress and avoids arbitrary responsibility. A student should be able to defend its trade-offs with evidence, not slogans.
